question: Suction olive harvesters cause extremely significant bird mortality and disturbance. The olive trees are stripped at night because cool temperatures help to preserve the olives’ aromatic compounds. The birds rest in the trees at night and are dazzled by the intense lighting of the machinery and become unable to effectively escape from the path of the harvesters.

If they do manage to fly away in time, they will often land on the next row of trees, only to suffer the same fate as another harvester follows. Scientists have confirmed that we are in the sixth mass extinction event, with the loss of an unprecedented number of species as a result of human activity. This nocturnal machine harvesting is completely at odds with the EU biodiversity strategy.

Some olive-growing regions have banned this nocturnal suction machine harvesting practice due to bird mortality and disturbance. Will the Commission introduce a blanket restriction on the practice given its cruelty, the fact that it undermines the EU biodiversity strategy and in the interests of a level playing field for all olive oil producers?
answer: EN behalf of the European Commission (27.3.2025) A blanket restriction on nocturnal olive harvesting methods in the EU has not been discussed. Instead, the issue has been tackled bilaterally with those Member States in which significant impacts were suspected. The Birds Directive1 provides a framework for the conservation of all wild birds.

In accordance its Article 5, Member States shall take the requisite measures to establish a general system of protection for all species of birds prohibiting in particular deliberate killing or capture by any method and deliberate disturbance of these birds particularly during the period of breeding and rearing.

Since 2019, the Commission engaged proactively in discussions with olive-producing Member States to address the issue of bird deaths caused by nocturnal olive harvesting. EU Pilots were launched to five Member States. Italy, Greece and France communicated that night harvesting of olives is not practiced in their territories. Portugal deemed the practice illegal and banned it.

In Spain, the Autonomous Communities of Andalucía, Castilla-La Mancha and Extremadura suspended the practice, and Spain informed the Commission this suspension would continue as long as no feasible and non-harmful alternative exists. Andalucía, by far the largest olive-producing region in the EU, has pledged to develop less harmful technical alternatives.

The Commission considers that significant progress has been made. The bans and suspensions in Portugal and Spain are crucial steps in the right direction. The Commission will continue to work with Member States to ensure that they comply with EU legislation and take the necessary measures to prevent bird deaths during olive harvesting.
1 Directive 2009/147/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on the
conservation of wild birds, OJ L 20, 26.1.2010, p. 7–25.
